alignment.note: Greek opens with paratactic καί ('and'), as does the Vulgate with Et, both clause-initial. The Peshitta instead uses the postpositive particle ܕܝܢ (deyn, 'but/now'), which falls in second position per Syriac syntax; the connective force is mildly adversative rather than purely additive.

Greek λίαν and Latin valde both intensify the adverb of time ('very early'). The Peshitta renders only ܒܫܦܪܐ ('at dawn') without an explicit intensifier, the temporal sense being already conveyed by the noun for daybreak.

Greek πρωΐ and Latin mane are temporal adverbs ('early/in the morning'). The Peshitta uses the prepositional noun ܒܫܦܪܐ ('at dawn'), from the root sh-p-r, expressing the same idea nominally rather than adverbially.

All three render 'on the first [day] of the week'; the Semitic idiom ܒܚܕ ܒܫܒܐ ('on one in the week') underlies the Greek τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων and Latin una sabbatorum, where the cardinal stands for the ordinal.
ἔρχονται / ܐܬܝ / veniunt — historic present 'they come'.
ἐπί / ad — preposition of motion 'to'; the Peshitta fuses the preposition into the following noun via the prefixed ܠ.

Greek τὸ μνημεῖον and Latin monumentum denote a single 'tomb/monument.' The Peshitta uses the construct phrase ܠܒܝܬ ܩܒܘܪܐ ('to the house of burial'), a typical Syriac periphrasis for a tomb compounding ܒܝܬ ('house') with the root q-b-r ('to bury').

Greek employs a genitive absolute (ἀνατείλαντος τοῦ ἡλίου, 'the sun having risen'); the Vulgate mirrors this with an ablative absolute orto... sole, adding jam ('already') for emphasis; the Peshitta uses a finite circumstantial clause introduced by ܟܕ ('when') with the verb ܕܢܚ ('rose'), a syntactically distinct but semantically equivalent temporal construction.
τοῦ ἡλίου / ܫܡܫܐ / sole — 'the sun', subject of the temporal clause.
